architects.name: Andrea Palladio
architects.bio: Born in Padua and trained as a stonemason, Palladio became the most influential architect of the Renaissance. His treatise The Four Books of Architecture (1570) spread his symmetrical, temple-fronted villas across Europe and the Americas, giving rise to Palladianism.

architects.name: Vincenzo Scamozzi
architects.bio: Born in Vicenza, Scamozzi inherited several of Palladio's unfinished projects after the master's death in 1580, among them the Teatro Olimpico and La Rotonda, where he designed the lower, Pantheon-like dome. His treatise L'idea della architettura universale (1615) and his only pupil, Baldassarre Longhena, carried Palladian ideas into the Venetian Baroque.

Four identical temple fronts face the four directions, so this hilltop house has no back.
Its architect died before it was finished; a younger colleague completed it with a lower dome.

summary.description: Begun in 1567 on a hilltop outside Vicenza for the retired cleric Paolo Almerico, La Rotonda is a perfectly symmetrical square block with a portico on every side and a domed hall at its heart. Palladio treated a private house like an ancient temple, and the result became one of the most copied buildings in Western architecture.
keyFeatures: Square plan with four identical Ionic porticoes
Central circular hall under a dome
Symmetry on both axes
Raised on a hill to command views on every side
funFacts: Palladio died in 1580; Vincenzo Scamozzi completed the villa and replaced the planned high dome with a lower one, open to the sky through an oculus like the Pantheon in Rome.
It inspired buildings from Chiswick House in London to country houses across Britain and America.
It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto'.

architects.name: Francesco Borromini
architects.bio: A stonemason's son from Bissone on Lake Lugano, Borromini spent his career in Rome, where his restless geometry and rippling walls made him the great rival of Gian Lorenzo Bernini. He built few, mostly small, churches, yet his inventive use of geometry shaped Baroque architecture across Europe.

The church closes the end of a courtyard belonging to the city's old university.
Its lantern ends in a corkscrew spiral, unique in its city.

summary.description: Borromini built this university church inside the existing courtyard of the Palazzo della Sapienza in Rome. Its plan grows from two interlocking equilateral triangles, and the star-shaped walls continue straight up into the dome, making the whole interior read as a single sculpted space.
keyFeatures: Star plan from two interlocking triangles
Walls and dome form one continuous surface
Almost colourless white interior that puts form first
Spiral lantern above a stepped dome
funFacts: The plan is often said to evoke a bee, the heraldic emblem of Pope Urban VIII's Barberini family.
Borromini was appointed architect of the Sapienza in 1632, reportedly on Bernini's recommendation.
Construction spanned the reigns of three popes, each of whom left his emblems on the building.

architects.name: Thomas Jefferson
architects.bio: Third President of the United States and principal author of the Declaration of Independence, Jefferson was also a self-taught architect. Learning largely from Palladio's books, he promoted classical architecture as a model for the new republic and designed the Virginia State Capitol and the University of Virginia.

hints.text: Its owner taught himself architecture, largely from the books of a Renaissance master.
Its owner spent four decades designing, demolishing and rebuilding it.
Its west front appears on the back of a coin.

summary.description: Jefferson began his hilltop plantation house in 1768 and spent forty years reshaping it, adding an octagonal dome after seeing the latest Neoclassical buildings in Paris. Built and maintained largely by enslaved people, it is today presented both as an architectural landmark and as a place to confront the history of slavery in the United States.
keyFeatures: Low octagonal dome over the west front
Temple-like porticoes in the manner of Palladio
Designed to look like a single storey, hiding the upper floors
Service wings tucked under terraces in the hillside
funFacts: The west front is pictured on the back of the US five-cent coin.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the University of Virginia, which Jefferson also designed.
Jefferson learned architecture largely from Palladio's Four Books, and the porticoes and proportions show it.

Church of Saint Francis of Assisi
São Francisco de Assis de Ouro Preto

architects.name: Antônio Francisco Lisboa
architects.bio: Son of a Portuguese architect and an enslaved African woman, Aleijadinho ('the little cripple') became the greatest artist of colonial Brazil, carving soapstone and wood across the gold-mining towns of Minas Gerais. A degenerative illness left him disabled, yet he kept working; his twelve soapstone prophets at Congonhas are his best-known sculptures.

photos.alt: White church with round bell towers and ornate stone carving around a green door
photos.credit: Photo: Paulo Bueno · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: The nave ceiling, painted by Manuel da Costa Ataíde.
photos.credit: Photo: Rezende1968 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It stands in an 18th-century gold-mining town.
Its circular bell towers were a novelty among the region's churches, and its frontispiece is carved in local soapstone.
Its designer was also the greatest sculptor of his colony, known by a nickname.

summary.description: Built for the Third Order of Saint Francis in Ouro Preto, the gold-rush capital of Minas Gerais, this church is the masterpiece of Aleijadinho, who designed both the building and much of its carving. Its curving façade, round towers and soapstone reliefs make it the defining work of the Barroco Mineiro, the late, Rococo-tinged Baroque of Brazil's mining towns.
keyFeatures: Circular bell towers set back from the façade
Soapstone frontispiece with a relief of Saint Francis receiving the stigmata
Oculus filled with a carved relief instead of a window
Nave ceiling painted by Manuel da Costa Ataíde
funFacts: The Third Order asked Lisbon for permission to build in 1752; approval only came in 1771, years after work had begun under a provisional licence.
Ouro Preto's historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Mosteiro de São Bento
aliases: Mosteiro de São Bento do Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Francisco Frias de Mesquita
architects.bio: A Portuguese military engineer sent to colonial Brazil, Frias de Mesquita designed fortifications and buildings along the coast. In 1617 he drew up the plans for São Bento in the plain Mannerist manner then current in Portugal.

architects.name: Frei Bernardo de São Bento Correia de Souza
architects.bio: A Benedictine friar and architect active in colonial Rio de Janeiro and one of the main figures behind the monastery's construction. He altered the original plan while it was being built, turning the single-nave church into one with three naves.

hints.text: Behind a plain, sober façade, almost every surface inside is covered in gilded carving.
It was paid for with income from sugar-cane estates given to the monks, and built by enslaved labourers.
It belongs to an order founded by Saint Benedict, on a hill above a South American harbour.

summary.description: Planned in 1617 and begun in 1633 on a hill overlooking Rio de Janeiro's harbour, the Benedictine monastery hides one of the richest Baroque interiors in Brazil behind a sober Mannerist façade. The church was enlarged to three naves during construction, and from the late 17th century its walls and vaults were covered in gilded carving.
keyFeatures: Mannerist façade with three entrance arches and a triangular pediment
Nave and chapels lined with gilded woodcarving (talha dourada)
Carving that runs from late Baroque to Rococo
Cloister completed in 1755
funFacts: Much of the carving in the nave and chancel was designed by the Benedictine Frei Domingos da Conceição (1643–1718).
The cloister was designed by the military engineer José Fernandes Pinto Alpoim and finished in 1755.

name: Theatro Municipal do Rio de Janeiro
aliases: Municipal Theatre of Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Francisco de Oliveira Passos
architects.bio: An engineer and later politician, the son of Rio's reforming mayor Francisco Pereira Passos. Under the pseudonym 'Áquila' he won the city's competition for a new municipal theatre.

architects.name: Albert Guilbert
architects.bio: French architect who worked with Oliveira Passos on the theatre's design, which takes Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra as its model.

photos.alt: Black-and-white street of wet cobblestones leading to an ornate domed building

hints.text: Its design takes a famous 19th-century Paris opera house as its model.
It was built in four and a half years, from 1905 to 1909, on a foundation of 1,180 wooden piles driven into waterlogged ground.
It faces a square nicknamed for its cinemas, in the centre of a former national capital.

summary.description: Rio's opera house was the showpiece of the city's Parisian-style remodelling in the early 1900s, when the new Avenida Central was cut through the old centre. Its eclectic, richly sculpted design follows Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra, and it opened in July 1909 with seats for 1,739 people.
keyFeatures: Eclectic façade modelled on the Paris Opéra
Green and gilded domes crowned by eagles
Names of European and Brazilian artists inscribed on the outer walls
Foundation of 1,180 wooden piles
funFacts: The winning design was entered under the pseudonym 'Áquila'.
President Nilo Peçanha inaugurated it on 14 July 1909.
It faces Cinelândia square, near the National Library and the National Museum of Fine Arts.

aliases: Church of Saint Francis of Assisi (Pampulha)

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

hints.text: Its roof is a row of parabolic concrete vaults, a form then used for aircraft hangars.
Church authorities refused for years to consecrate it, objecting to its form and to a mural showing a dog beside Saint Francis.
It belongs to a lakeside ensemble built in the 1940s for a mayor who later became president.

summary.description: The last building of the Pampulha ensemble that Niemeyer designed for Juscelino Kubitschek, then mayor of Belo Horizonte, this small chapel abandons the slab-on-pilotis formula for a row of parabolic concrete vaults that are structure and enclosure at once. Its free curves announced a distinctly Brazilian modernism.
keyFeatures: Parabolic reinforced-concrete vaults, a form then used for hangars
Vaults acting as both structure and walls
Freestanding lattice bell tower
Tile murals by Cândido Portinari and Paulo Werneck
funFacts: Inside, Portinari's fourteen Stations of the Cross are considered among his most important works.
The structure was calculated by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo, Niemeyer's long-time collaborator.
The Pampulha Modern Ensemble became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

hints.text: It was built in about fourteen months, one of the first buildings of a brand-new capital city.
It is the official residence of a head of state.
Its name comes from a question its client asked: what is the new capital, if not the dawn of a new day for Brazil?

summary.description: Built in about fourteen months, from April 1957 to June 1958, the official residence of the President of Brazil was one of the first buildings of the new capital. A long glass box sits behind a portico of sculptural white columns whose curves became a symbol of Brasília.
keyFeatures: Glass box set back behind a colonnade
Curving columns tapering to fine points
Reflecting pool in front
Long, low proportions near the shore of Lake Paranoá
funFacts: Every Brazilian president since Juscelino Kubitschek has lived there.
A golden wall inside carries a 1956 quotation by Kubitschek about the new capital.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

hints.text: It opened in 1960, the year its city became a national capital.
The low dome shelters one chamber of the legislature; the upturned bowl, the other.
Its two office towers are linked to form an H.

summary.description: Inaugurated with the new capital in 1960, Brazil's parliament closes the Esplanade of Ministries at the Square of the Three Powers. Niemeyer set the two houses on a long horizontal platform, the Senate under a dome and the Chamber of Deputies in an upturned bowl, with twin 28-storey office towers rising between them.
keyFeatures: Horizontal platform whose roof is a raised plaza
Dome over the Federal Senate
Upturned bowl over the Chamber of Deputies
Twin office towers linked to form an H
funFacts: In Rio de Janeiro the two houses had sat in separate buildings; Brasília joined them in one palace.
The structure was designed by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo.
Brasília is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Museu de Arte de São Paulo
aliases: Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand

architects.name: Lina Bo Bardi
architects.bio: Born Achillina Bo in Rome, she moved to Brazil in 1946 with her husband, the critic and dealer Pietro Maria Bardi. Fascinated by Brazilian popular culture, she joined modernist rigour to a raw, humane architecture, from MASP to SESC Pompéia.

hints.text: Its galleries are lifted into a glass box hung between two great frames, leaving a public plaza beneath.
Its architect displayed the paintings on glass easels so they seemed to float in the gallery.
Its collection of European art is considered one of the finest in the Southern Hemisphere.

summary.description: On the site of the old Trianon belvedere on Avenida Paulista, Lina Bo Bardi lifted the museum's galleries into a glass and concrete box hung between two great frames. Beneath it, a covered public plaza about 74 metres long is left open to the city.
keyFeatures: Gallery box spanning about 74 metres between two pairs of pillars
Free public plaza beneath (the vão livre)
Exposed concrete and glass
Paintings shown on transparent easels
funFacts: Bo Bardi displayed the paintings on glass and concrete easels so they seemed to float in the gallery; the museum brought them back in 2015.
The museum opened in 1947 in a downtown building and moved here in 1968.
Queen Elizabeth II attended its inauguration in 1968.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

hints.text: Its structure is a hyperboloid of sixteen curved concrete columns.
Visitors enter through a low, dark passage and emerge into coloured light.
It was dedicated in 1970 in a capital founded only ten years earlier.

summary.description: A hyperboloid of sixteen curved concrete columns, each weighing about 90 tonnes, rises from a circular base like hands reaching towards the sky. Visitors enter through a dark, low passage and emerge into a nave filled with coloured light.
keyFeatures: Hyperboloid of 16 concrete columns
Glass between the ribs, with stained glass by Marianne Peretti (1990)
Entrance through a low, dark passage
Reflecting pool around the building
funFacts: Three angels by Alfredo Ceschiatti hang from steel cables over the nave.
It was engineered by Joaquim Cardozo and dedicated on 31 May 1970.

name: Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo

architects.name: Ramos de Azevedo
aliases: Francisco de Paula Ramos de Azevedo
architects.bio: The most prolific architect of turn-of-the-century São Paulo, Ramos de Azevedo ran the office behind many of the city's public buildings and directed the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios, for which this building was designed.

architects.name: Domiziano Rossi
architects.bio: Ramos de Azevedo's main collaborator, who designed the Liceu building with him in the Italian eclectic manner.

architects.name: Paulo Mendes da Rocha
architects.bio: Born in Vitória and based in São Paulo, Mendes da Rocha was a leading figure of the Paulista School, known for bold, economical concrete structures. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2006 and the Venice Biennale's Golden Lion in 2016.

architects.name: Eduardo Colonelli
architects.bio: São Paulo architect who led the 1993–98 renovation with Paulo Mendes da Rocha and Weliton Ricoy Torres.

architects.name: Weliton Ricoy Torres
architects.bio: São Paulo architect, co-author of the 1993–98 renovation with Paulo Mendes da Rocha and Eduardo Colonelli.

hints.text: Its brick walls were never covered with the plaster that was planned.
It was built for a school of arts and crafts and opened, still unfinished, in 1900.
It houses the oldest art museum in the largest city of its country.

summary.description: Designed by Ramos de Azevedo and Domiziano Rossi for the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios, this eclectic brick building beside the Jardim da Luz opened unfinished in 1900 and became the home of São Paulo's oldest art museum, founded in 1905. Between 1993 and 1998 Paulo Mendes da Rocha, with Eduardo Colonelli and Weliton Ricoy Torres, transformed it: the courtyards were roofed with glass and crossed by metal walkways, and the bare brick was left on show.
keyFeatures: Exposed brick walls, never plastered
Two inner courtyards roofed in glass during the renovation
Metal walkways crossing the courtyards
Side loggias and windows facing the Jardim da Luz
funFacts: The renovation won the Mies van der Rohe Prize for Latin America.
It was listed as a heritage building in 1982, part of the turn-of-the-century ensemble of the Luz district.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

photos.caption: The round gallery inside the saucer.
photos.credit: Photo: Rodrigo Soldon · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its gallery is a single saucer-shaped volume resting on one cylindrical support.
Its architect said it rises from its pool 'like a flower'.
It rises 16 metres from a reflecting pool on a clifftop, looking across a bay to a famous granite peak.

summary.description: Perched on a rocky point above Boa Viagem beach, Niemeyer's museum rises from a single cylindrical base out of its reflecting pool. The saucer-shaped gallery, 50 metres across, looks over Guanabara Bay to Rio de Janeiro and Sugarloaf Mountain.
keyFeatures: Saucer-shaped volume on a single cylindrical support
Reflecting pool of 817 m² around the base
Continuous band of windows with views across the bay
Sculptural access ramp
funFacts: Niemeyer said it rises from its pool 'like a flower'.
It has often been likened to a UFO.

Its long main building was designed by the same architect in 1967 as an education institute and opened in 1978.
It was completed when its architect was 95, and now bears his name.

summary.description: In 2002 Curitiba turned a 1967 Niemeyer building, designed as an education institute, into a museum. The next year the architect, then 95, added the annex that gave it its nickname: an eye-shaped gallery of glass and steel raised on a single yellow pillar, set in grounds landscaped by Roberto Burle Marx.
keyFeatures: Eye-shaped annex on a single pillar
Glass and steel façades lighting the exhibition space
Sinuous access ramps
Long modernist main building
funFacts: It opened in 2002 as the Novo Museu and took its architect's name in 2003.
Inside the 'eye', a spiral stair links the levels.

architects.name: Antoni Gaudí
architects.bio: Born in 1852 in the Reus area of Catalonia, Gaudí developed an architecture whose structure is drawn from nature, with catenary arches, branching columns and trencadís mosaic, and became the emblem of Catalan Modernisme. He gave his last years entirely to the Sagrada Família and died in 1926 after being struck by a tram. Seven of his works form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

It was its architect's first major commission: a summer house for a stock and currency broker.
It stands in a former town now absorbed into a large Mediterranean port city.

summary.description: Gaudí's first major house was built in 1883–85 as a summer residence for Manuel Vicens, a stock and currency broker, in what was then the town of Gràcia. Its brick and tile walls draw on Mudéjar, Persian and Japanese sources, in an orientalist style Gaudí made his own.
keyFeatures: Green and white chequered ceramic tiles
Brick walls with Mudéjar-inspired decoration
Ornate ceilings and oriental-style rooms
Cast-iron railings with palm-leaf motifs
funFacts: Gaudí studied Owen Jones's drawings of the Alhambra while developing its oriental style.
It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Works of Antoni Gaudí'.

Carriages drove in through gates shaped as parabolic arches, with ironwork resembling seaweed.
Its roof bristles with chimneys clad in broken-tile mosaic.

summary.description: Built in 1886–88 in Barcelona's old town for the industrialist Eusebi Güell, Gaudí's great patron, this town palace is organised around a tall central hall rising to a dome. Above, chimneys clad in broken-tile mosaic crown the roof.
keyFeatures: Parabolic entrance arches with wrought-iron gates
Central hall rising to a perforated dome
Stables in the basement
Rooftop chimneys covered in trencadís
funFacts: Guests arrived in horse-drawn carriages, driving straight in through the front gates.
It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Works of Antoni Gaudí'.

architects.name: Antoni Gaudí
architects.bio: Born in 1852 in the Reus area of Catalonia, Gaudí developed an architecture whose structure is drawn from nature, with catenary arches, branching columns and trencadís mosaic, and became the emblem of Catalan Modernisme. He gave his last years entirely to the Sagrada Família and died in 1926 after being struck by a tram. Seven of his works form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

photos.alt: Fairy-tale gatehouse with a mosaic-covered roof and a tall tiled spire
photos.credit: Photo: Txllxt TxllxT · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Ceiling of white broken-tile mosaic set with a large round multicoloured medallion
photos.caption: Mosaic medallions on the ceiling of the hall of columns.
photos.credit: Photo: Jorge Franganillo · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its paths are carried on leaning colonnades of rough rubble stone.
It was planned as a garden city for wealthy families, but only two houses were built.
Its terrace is edged by a long serpentine bench covered in broken-tile mosaic.

summary.description: Count Eusebi Güell commissioned Gaudí to lay out a hillside estate of houses in the spirit of the English garden city. Built between 1900 and 1914, the scheme failed as housing, and the grounds opened as a public park in 1926: viaducts of rough stone, gatehouses, a hall of columns beneath a great terrace, and a serpentine mosaic bench.
keyFeatures: Viaducts and leaning colonnades of rubble stone
Two gatehouse pavilions at the entrance
Hall of columns under the main terrace
Serpentine bench covered in trencadís
funFacts: The serpentine bench was designed by Gaudí's collaborator Josep Maria Jujol.
Güell himself moved onto the estate in 1906 to promote it.

architects.name: Antoni Gaudí
architects.bio: Born in 1852 in the Reus area of Catalonia, Gaudí developed an architecture whose structure is drawn from nature, with catenary arches, branching columns and trencadís mosaic, and became the emblem of Catalan Modernisme. He gave his last years entirely to the Sagrada Família and died in 1926 after being struck by a tram. Seven of his works form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

drawings.label: Façade and section (1904)
drawings.alt: Hand-drawn elevation of a narrow house front with bulging windows, beside its section
drawings.credit: Antoni Gaudí · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Mike McBey · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Curving plaster wall pierced by two rounded windows of leaded glass
photos.caption: Rounded windows along the stairwell.
photos.credit: Photo: Richard Mortel · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was not a new building: its architect transformed an existing house from 1877.
Locals call it the House of Bones, after its bone-like columns and mask-like balconies.
Its roof, covered in scale-like tiles, is often likened to the back of a dragon.

summary.description: In 1904 the textile industrialist Josep Batlló hired Gaudí to transform his 1877 house on the Passeig de Gràcia. Finished in 1906, it has a façade of broken-tile mosaic shading from gold to blue-green, mask-like balconies, bone-like columns and a roof that recalls the back of a dragon.
keyFeatures: Trencadís mosaic façade
Mask-like balconies and bone-like columns
Arched, scaly roof
Few straight lines anywhere
funFacts: Barcelona's City Council shortlisted it for the 1906 best building award, which went to another architect.
Locals call it Casa dels Ossos, the House of Bones.

architects.name: Antoni Gaudí
architects.bio: Born in 1852 in the Reus area of Catalonia, Gaudí developed an architecture whose structure is drawn from nature, with catenary arches, branching columns and trencadís mosaic, and became the emblem of Catalan Modernisme. He gave his last years entirely to the Sagrada Família and died in 1926 after being struck by a tram. Seven of his works form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

photos.caption: A painted entrance hall.
photos.credit: Photo: Alvesgaspar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its stone façade carries no load: columns hold up the floors, so walls inside could go anywhere.
Its city mocked it with a nickname meaning 'the stone quarry', and the name stuck.
It was its architect's last private house, finished in 1912.

summary.description: Gaudí's last private house, built in 1906–12 for Pere Milà and Roser Segimon, wraps around two courtyards behind an undulating stone façade with twisting wrought-iron balconies. Columns carry the floors so that interior walls can go anywhere, and an underground garage and a sculpted roof terrace complete a building far ahead of its time.
keyFeatures: Self-supporting, undulating stone façade
Free floor plans on a column structure
Two large inner courtyards
Roof terrace of sculpted chimneys and stair towers
funFacts: Barcelona mocked it as 'La Pedrera', the stone quarry, and the nickname stuck.
Its wrought-iron balconies were designed by Josep Maria Jujol.
Gaudí certified the building complete on 31 October 1912.

name: Sagrada Família
aliases: Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família

architects.name: Antoni Gaudí
architects.bio: Born in 1852 in the Reus area of Catalonia, Gaudí developed an architecture whose structure is drawn from nature, with catenary arches, branching columns and trencadís mosaic, and became the emblem of Catalan Modernisme. He gave his last years entirely to the Sagrada Família and died in 1926 after being struck by a tram. Seven of his works form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

drawings.label: Plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a large cross-shaped church with a many-aisled nave, a rounded apse and broad stairs at the front
drawings.credit: Antoni Gaudí · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Michielverbeek · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Columns branch like trees to hold up the vaults.
photos.credit: Photo: Triptychon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Begun in 1882, it is still being built, paid for entirely by donations.
Its columns branch like trees to carry the vaults.
Its architect devoted his last years entirely to it and is buried in its crypt.

summary.description: Begun in 1882 to a conventional Gothic Revival design, the expiatory church passed in 1883 to Gaudí, who reshaped it into a vast, forest-like basilica and worked on it until his death in 1926. Construction continues, funded by donations; in 2026 its central Tower of Jesus Christ reached 172.5 metres, making it the world's tallest church.
keyFeatures: Branching, tree-like columns
Three façades: Nativity, Passion and Glory
Towers for the apostles, the evangelists, Mary and Jesus
Geometry of hyperboloids and helicoids
funFacts: Its first architect, Francisco de Paula del Villar, resigned in 1883.
Pope Benedict XVI consecrated it as a basilica on 7 November 2010.
The central tower was blessed on 10 June 2026, a hundred years after Gaudí's death.

architects.name: Victor Horta
architects.bio: Born in Ghent, Horta designed a series of Brussels town houses in the 1890s that made him the pioneer of Art Nouveau architecture, with open plans, exposed iron and whiplash ornament. Four of them, including the Hôtel Tassel and his own house, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

photos.alt: Narrow stone town-house front with a projecting bow window of iron and glass
photos.credit: Photo: Kat_hly.1608 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Curving stair with whiplash ironwork, slender iron column and painted swirling walls
photos.caption: The stair hall at the heart of the house.
photos.credit: Photo: Henry Townsend · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for a scientist and university professor, and is counted among the very first buildings of its style.
Instead of a row of dark rooms, its rooms are arranged around a central stair hall.
It stands in a European capital known for its comic strips and its parliament of the Union.

summary.description: Designed by Victor Horta for the scientist and professor Émile Tassel and built in 1892–93, this Brussels town house is considered one of the first Art Nouveau buildings. Instead of the usual row of dark rooms, Horta arranged the house around a central stair hall, and let exposed iron and whiplash ornament flow through it.
keyFeatures: Central stair hall linking the different levels
Exposed iron columns, inside and on the façade
Whiplash ornament in iron, mosaic and paint
Projecting bow window
funFacts: It strongly influenced the French Art Nouveau architect Hector Guimard.
With three other Horta town houses, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

name: Glasgow School of Art
aliases: Glasgow School of Art Mackintosh Building

architects.name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
architects.bio: Glasgow architect, designer and watercolourist and the leading figure of the Glasgow Style. Working with the firm Honeyman & Keppie, he won the 1896 competition for the School of Art; late in life he gave up architecture to paint watercolours in France.

architects.name: Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh
architects.bio: Artist and designer, one of 'The Four' of the Glasgow Style, and Charles Rennie Mackintosh's wife and collaborator.

photos.alt: Stone façade with large studio windows, an off-centre entrance and curving iron railings
photos.credit: Photo: Dave & Margie Hill / Kleerup · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Black-and-white room with tall-backed dark chairs around a long table
photos.caption: The Board Room, photographed in 1964.
photos.credit: Photo: Alan Murray-Rust · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built in two phases, finished in 1899 and 1909.
Its huge north-facing windows light painting studios.
It was gutted by fire twice, in 2014 and 2018.

summary.description: Charles Rennie Mackintosh won the 1896 competition for the school's new building on Garnethill, which went up in two phases, completed in 1899 and 1909. Its huge north-facing studio windows, stark stone masses and inventive ironwork made it a landmark of early modern design. It was badly damaged by fire in 2014 and gutted by a second fire in 2018.
keyFeatures: Large north-facing studio windows
Asymmetrical stone façade with an off-centre entrance
Decorative wrought-iron brackets and railings
Library of timber columns and beams, lost in the 2014 fire
funFacts: Its library, one of Mackintosh's finest interiors, was destroyed in the 2014 fire.
Six recent Turner Prize winners studied at the school.

architects.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
architects.bio: Over a career of some seventy years Wright developed an 'organic architecture' rooted in landscape, from the low, horizontal Prairie houses of the 1900s to Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum. Eight of his buildings form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

drawings.label: Longitudinal section and south elevation
drawings.alt: Long, low house in section and elevation, with wide overhanging roofs

photos.alt: Long, low brick house with deep overhanging roofs and bands of windows
photos.credit: Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Bedroom with wooden furniture and a row of leaded art-glass windows
photos.caption: A bedroom lit by art-glass windows.
photos.credit: Photo: w_lemay · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its roofs cantilever far beyond the walls, and its long horizontal lines echo the flat Midwestern prairie.
It was built for a manufacturing executive and now belongs to a university.
It helped popularise picture windows, deep eaves and attached garages.

summary.description: Completed in 1910 for the manufacturing executive Frederick C. Robie in Chicago's Hyde Park, this is often called the finest of Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie houses. Its low brick walls, bands of art-glass windows and roofs cantilevered far beyond the walls stretch the house along its corner plot.
keyFeatures: Long, low horizontal lines
Roofs cantilevered far beyond the walls
Bands of art-glass windows
Terraces on several levels
funFacts: It helped popularise picture windows, deep eaves and attached garages in American houses.
It now belongs to the University of Chicago and is part of the UNESCO site 'The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright'.
It was one of the last buildings Wright designed at his Oak Park studio.

architects.name: Adolf Loos
architects.bio: Viennese architect and polemicist whose essay 'Ornament and Crime' attacked decoration as wasteful. His buildings pair plain exteriors with rich materials inside, and his Raumplan arranged rooms at different heights.

drawings.label: Ground floor plan
drawings.alt: Irregular corner-plot plan with a shop floor, columns and stairs
drawings.credit: FiliGelpi03 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section
drawings.alt: Section through a multi-storey building: a shop below, plain apartment floors above
drawings.credit: FiliGelpi03 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Tilman2007 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Marble-lined entrance passage with glass doors
photos.caption: Rich marble lines the ground-floor entrance.
photos.credit: Photo: Thomas Ledl · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its plain upper floors caused such a scandal that the architect had to add flower boxes to the windows.
It was built for a firm of gentlemen's tailors, opposite an imperial palace.
Its architect wrote a famous essay attacking ornament.

summary.description: Built for the tailors Goldman & Salatsch on Vienna's Michaelerplatz, opposite the imperial Hofburg, the building contrasts a base of green Cipollino marble with completely plain upper floors. In 1910 the bare façade caused a public scandal; construction resumed only after Loos agreed to add window boxes with flowers.
keyFeatures: Ground floor and mezzanine clad in green marble
Unornamented white upper storeys
Classical columns at the shop entrance
Window boxes added to quiet the critics
funFacts: Emperor Franz Joseph reportedly kept the Hofburg's curtains closed so he would not have to see it.
One newspaper called it a 'dung heap' before the flower boxes were added.

architects.name: Walter Gropius
architects.bio: After working for Peter Behrens, Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 and moved it to Dessau in 1925. He emigrated in the 1930s and taught at Harvard, spreading modernist teaching in America.

architects.name: Adolf Meyer
architects.bio: Gropius's partner in his early practice and co-designer of the Fagus Factory; he later taught at the Bauhaus and became Frankfurt's city building director.

photos.alt: Three-storey building whose glass walls wrap around a corner with no supporting pillar
photos.credit: Photo: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Stair hall with black-banded walls and a stair rising beside a glazed corner
photos.caption: The main stair, beside the glass corner.
photos.credit: Photo: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its glass walls wrap around a corner with no supporting pillar.
Its owner made shoe lasts and wanted a building that broke with the past.
Both its architects had worked for the designer of a famous Berlin turbine hall.

summary.description: Built in 1911–13 for Carl Benscheidt's shoe-last company, the factory's main block wraps glass walls around its corners with no supporting pillar, turning the wall into a thin screen hung between recessed brick piers. It reversed the heavy corners of Behrens's AEG turbine hall, where both of its architects had worked.
keyFeatures: Glass curtain walls running the full height
Corners left free of supports
Brick piers set back behind the glass
Additions and interiors completed in 1925
funFacts: Gropius described the walls as 'mere screens stretched between the upright columns of the framework'.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.
The factory still makes shoe lasts.

architects.name: Erich Mendelsohn
architects.bio: Mendelsohn sketched fluid, dynamic buildings while serving in the First World War; the Einstein Tower made his name, followed by department stores in Germany. He left in 1933, working in Britain, Palestine and the United States.

photos.alt: Smooth, curving white tower topped by a small dome, among trees
photos.credit: Photo: Muck · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Large telescope mirror mounted in a white instrument chamber
photos.caption: Inside, mirrors send sunlight down a shaft to the laboratory.
photos.credit: Photo: Bautsch · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built to test a famous scientist's theory of relativity by observing the Sun.
Its flowing form was imagined in concrete, but much of it is brick covered in stucco.
It is still a working solar observatory.

summary.description: Designed by Erich Mendelsohn and built in 1919–21 on the Telegraphenberg in Potsdam, this solar observatory houses a telescope built to test Albert Einstein's theory of relativity. Its flowing, sculptural form was imagined in concrete, but wartime shortages meant much of it was built in brick covered with stucco.
keyFeatures: Fluid, sculptural Expressionist form
Dome housing the coelostat at the top
Shaft sending light down to a basement laboratory
Brick and stucco shaped to look like poured concrete
funFacts: Einstein never worked there, but he supported its construction.
It is still a working solar observatory.
The young Richard Neutra was on Mendelsohn's staff during the project.

architects.name: Gerrit Rietveld
architects.bio: A cabinetmaker turned architect, Rietveld joined the De Stijl movement and designed the Red and Blue Chair before building this house with Truus Schröder. He went on to a long career in Utrecht.

photos.alt: Small house of overlapping white and grey planes at the end of a brick terrace
photos.credit: Photo: Luis Guillermo R. · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Simple table and red chair in a room with windows on two sides
photos.caption: The upper floor, with its corner windows.
photos.credit: Photo: G.oorthuys · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its upper floor can be one open space or divided into rooms with sliding and revolving panels.
It sits at the end of a terrace of brick houses but ignores them completely.
Its designer, trained as a cabinetmaker, is also famous for a red and blue chair.

summary.description: Built in 1924 for Truus Schröder-Schräder and her three children at the end of a brick terrace in Utrecht, the house is the purest built expression of De Stijl: free-floating planes, lines and primary colours. Its upper floor can be opened into one space or divided into rooms with sliding and revolving panels.
keyFeatures: Composition of independent planes and lines
Primary colours with white, grey and black
Flexible upper floor with sliding partitions
Corner windows that open to remove the corner entirely
funFacts: It included a garage, though Truus Schröder did not own a car.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

architects.name: Walter Gropius
architects.bio: After working for Peter Behrens, Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 and moved it to Dessau in 1925. He emigrated in the 1930s and taught at Harvard, spreading modernist teaching in America.

photos.alt: Workshop wing with a continuous glass curtain wall, beside a lower white wing
photos.credit: Photo: Spyrosdrakopoulos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Assembly hall with rows of tubular lamps hanging from a ribbed ceiling
photos.caption: The assembly hall.
photos.credit: Photo: James Steakley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its wings for workshops, classrooms and student studios are linked by a two-storey bridge over a road.
Its workshop wing is wrapped in a continuous glass curtain wall.
It was built when a famous art and design school moved here from Weimar in 1925.

summary.description: Built in 1925–26 when the Bauhaus school moved from Weimar to Dessau, Gropius's building gives each function its own wing: a workshop block behind a glass curtain wall, a technical school, and a five-storey studio house for students, joined by a bridge over the road and a low wing with the hall and canteen.
keyFeatures: Glass curtain wall of the workshop wing
Pinwheel plan of separate wings
Two-storey bridge spanning a road
Studio house with small balconies
funFacts: The 28 studios in the five-storey Prellerhaus were living and working space for students and young masters.
Curtains needed for sun protection spoiled the intended transparency of the glass wall.
It has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.

architects.name: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
architects.bio: A former assistant of Peter Behrens, Mies reduced architecture to steel, glass and fine materials ('less is more'). Last director of the Bauhaus, he emigrated to Chicago, where he built the Illinois Institute of Technology campus and later the Seagram Building in New York.

architects.name: Lilly Reich
architects.bio: Designer and Mies's close collaborator in the late 1920s and 1930s, co-author of the pavilion and its furniture, and head of the Bauhaus weaving and interior workshops.

photos.alt: Low pavilion of stone walls and glass under a flat roof, beside a pool
photos.credit: Photo: Ashley Pomeroy at English Wikipedia · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Free-standing walls of onyx and glass.
photos.credit: Photo: No machine-readable author provided. Mcginnly assumed (based on copyright claims). · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It was built for an international exposition and held no exhibits, only the building itself.
It was demolished less than a year after it opened, and rebuilt on the same site in 1986.
A famous steel and leather chair was designed for it.

summary.description: Built as Germany's pavilion for the 1929 International Exposition in Barcelona, it held no exhibits: only the building itself, a sculpture by Georg Kolbe and furniture designed for it. Free-standing walls of marble, onyx and tinted glass divide a flowing space under a thin flat roof on slender steel columns.
keyFeatures: Thin flat roof on cruciform steel columns
Free-standing walls of marble, onyx and glass
Travertine plinth and reflecting pools
Open, flowing plan
funFacts: The Barcelona chair was designed for it and is still made today.
It was torn down in early 1930 and reconstructed in 1986.

architects.name: Isidore of Miletus
architects.bio: Greek geometer and engineer from Miletus, commissioned by Emperor Justinian I to design the new cathedral of Constantinople with Anthemius of Tralles.

architects.name: Anthemius of Tralles
architects.bio: Greek mathematician and engineer from Tralles in Asia Minor, co-designer of Hagia Sophia for Emperor Justinian I.

drawings.alt: Plan of a huge rectangular church with a central square crowned by a circle and half-domes at each end
drawings.credit: 19th-century engraving · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.credit: 19th-century engraving · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

photos.credit: Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: A dome ringed by windows seems to float over the nave.
photos.credit: Photo: Kemal KOZBAEV · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: For nearly a thousand years it enclosed the largest interior space in the world.
It has been a cathedral, a mosque, a museum, and a mosque again.
Its dome rests on a ring of forty windows, so it seems to float.

summary.description: Built for Emperor Justinian I between 532 and 537 and designed by the geometers Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles, Hagia Sophia was the cathedral of Constantinople. Its vast dome, one of the first carried on pendentives, rests on a ring of windows. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1935, and a mosque again in 2020.
keyFeatures: Central dome on pendentives
Ring of 40 windows at the base of the dome
Half-domes extending the central space
Minarets added after 1453
funFacts: It became the model for Ottoman mosques a thousand years later.
It was Turkey's most visited tourist attraction in 2019.

architects.name: Filippo Brunelleschi
architects.bio: Trained as a goldsmith, Brunelleschi is credited with rediscovering linear perspective and with founding Renaissance architecture through works such as the Foundling Hospital and San Lorenzo in Florence. His dome solved a problem that had defeated builders for decades.

photos.alt: Gothic nave of tall pointed arches leading to a domed octagon
photos.caption: The nave leads to a vast octagonal crossing.
photos.credit: Photo: Zde · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: Its builder won a competition against the goldsmith Lorenzo Ghiberti.
It was built without the full timber centring normally used to support a dome during construction.
It is still the largest masonry dome ever built.

summary.description: The cathedral of Florence was begun in 1296 to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, but its huge octagonal crossing stood open for decades. Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome between 1420 and 1436 without the timber centring normally used, and it remains the largest masonry dome ever built.
keyFeatures: Octagonal dome of two shells
Eight white marble ribs over red tile
Built without full timber centring
Lantern crowning the dome
funFacts: Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral on 25 March 1436.
Guillaume Dufay's motet Nuper rosarum flores was written for the consecration.
Brunelleschi and Ghiberti were appointed jointly, a rivalry that lasted for years.

name: Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio

architects.name: Donato Bramante
architects.bio: Born near Urbino, Bramante worked in Milan before moving to Rome in 1499. The Tempietto launched the High Renaissance there, and in 1503 Pope Julius II charged him with rebuilding St Peter's Basilica.

photos.alt: Round temple with a ring of columns and a dome, beside a bell tower
photos.credit: Photo: JTSH26 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt: Looking up into a small stone dome ringed by statues in shell-headed niches
photos.caption: Inside the tiny dome.
photos.credit: Photo: NateBergin · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.text: It marks the spot where Saint Peter was traditionally believed to have been martyred.
Despite its tiny size, it follows ancient Roman proportions so strictly that it launched a new style in its city.
Its architect later began the rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica.

summary.description: Commissioned around 1502 for the courtyard of San Pietro in Montorio on the Janiculum, Bramante's tiny round temple marks the traditional site of Saint Peter's martyrdom. Ringed by Doric columns and crowned by a dome, it applies ancient Roman proportions so rigorously that it is seen as the beginning of the High Renaissance in Rome.
keyFeatures: Circular plan with a peristyle of Doric columns
Hemispherical dome on a drum
Balustrade above the colonnade
Strict classical proportions at small scale
funFacts: Serlio's engraving shows that Bramante planned to set it in a circular colonnaded courtyard, never built.
It was commissioned by Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, or possibly by Pope Julius II.

architects.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
architects.bio: Over a career of some seventy years Wright developed an 'organic architecture' rooted in landscape, from the low, horizontal Prairie houses of the 1900s to Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum. Eight of his buildings form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
